rv.q: The sheer brio of this adaptation, and the deep conviction of the cast, absolutely carry it off.

It might frustrate classical scholars too. Fine, they’ll say, this queen of Athens is now a senior politician with homes in Holland Park and Suffolk, the absent Theseus is now a jaunty diplomat called Hugo, and he is played by Paul Chahidi (the vicar from This Country), in the despairingly decent register at which he excels.
A crack cast makes this soapy saga all the more enjoyable.
Whatever your verdict, the visionary elan of the night is not in question.
Stone’s dialogue is sparky, hilarious and lightning-quick, its strands interlocking and tangling together like electric cables.
It doesn’t quite hang together, but it’s a hell of a ride.
This is potentially fruitful terrain but the play’s tone repeatedly switches from comedy to serious drama, which brings confusion over what it is trying to say or do.
Stone’s dialogue is too gauche and bombastic to give any real nuance to Helen’s feelings and actions.
It really is a stunning piece of theatre.
I think the superb staging, lighting and commitment of the cast make the show one of the best things I’ve ever seen at the National.
Propped up with powerhouse performances, this Phaedra is a savage beauty as terrifying as it is tragic.
This is meaty, pugilistic, wrenching drama, anchored by an unmissable performance by McTeer.
This Phaedra is inconsistent, over-gimmicky and occasionally baffling. However, its plus points outnumber its flaws and it achieves a strange and seductive quality that imprints itself on the mind.
It all adds up to a remarkable tour de force.
It's a shame the text couldn't be as revolutionary as the revolving stage it's on.
The abrupt descent into emotional darkness is convincing largely due to the astonishingly confident performances.

cn.t: Stone's audacious modern reimagining of the Greek myth divides critics. McTeer's formidable performance anchors this contemporary political satire, though some find the adaptation's dialogue and execution fall short of its ambitious premise.
